Gulliver's Travels. Jonathan Swift's 1726 satirical voyage narrative follows Lemuel Gulliver on four journeys to fantastical lands. He travels to Lilliput, inhabited by tiny people; Brobdingnag, inhabited by giants; Laputa, a land of obsessed scholars; and the country of the Houyhnhnms, governed by rational horses. It is a cutting political allegory and philosophical satire that exposes human folly, hypocrisy, and moral degradation beneath the veneer of civilization.

Published anonymously in 1726, Gulliver's Travels was initially read as a straightforward adventure tale. But it was later recognized as Swift's most elaborate satire of contemporary politics, science, and human nature. His first voyage to Lilliput contains thinly veiled references to eighteenth-century British politics, with the diminutive Lilliputians parodying courtly intrigue and petty faction. The second voyage to Brobdingnag inverts the scale, forcing Gulliver and the reader to see humanity from the perspective of the giants, who regard human customs and politics with disgust.

Laputa satirizes the Royal Society and contemporary scientific obsessions. Its inhabitants are so absorbed in abstract mathematics and music that they neglect practical life and governance. The final voyage to the land of the Houyhnhnms is Swift's harshest critique: rational horses govern their society while debased humans, called Yahoos, represent humanity stripped of reason and virtue.

Gulliver's transformation throughout the novel—from confident observer to horrified misanthrope—reflects Swift's growing contempt for human civilization itself. Despite its fantastical content, the prose is matter-of-fact and journalistic, which lends the work an unsettling plausibility.
